questions.q: Which of the following pipelines will display the count of visible (non‑hidden) entries in the current user's home directory?
questions.why: ‘ls $HOME’ lists only non‑hidden items; piping to wc -l counts the lines, giving the number of visible entries.

questions.q: To see the used and available space on the root partition in a human‑readable format, which command should you run?
questions.why: ‘df -h /’ reports filesystem size, used space, and free space for the specified mount point in human‑readable units.

questions.q: In a command synopsis like "ls [options] [files]", what do the square brackets signify?
options: The enclosed items are optional and may be omitted.
The enclosed items are mandatory arguments.
The brackets must be typed literally when entering the command.
The brackets indicate a choice between the listed items.
questions.why: Square brackets in command syntax denote optional components; the user may include or omit them.

questions.q: Which of the following paths is an absolute path in a Linux filesystem?
questions.why: An absolute path starts with a leading slash, so /etc/passwd is absolute; the others are relative.

questions.q: If the current working directory is /home/user/projects, what absolute directory does the relative path ".." refer to?
questions.why: ".." means the parent directory, so from /home/user/projects it resolves to /home/user.

questions.q: Which command will change the shell’s current directory to the directory linuxpocketguide located in the user’s home directory?
questions.why: The tilde (~) expands to the user’s home directory, so cd ~/linuxpocketguide changes to that path.

questions.q: Which pattern will correctly match the hidden file named .profile in the current directory?
questions.why: Wildcards do not match a leading period unless the period is typed explicitly; .pro* matches .profile while *profile would miss the hidden file.

questions.q: What will the command `echo file{1,2,3}.txt` display?
questions.why: Brace expansion creates separate arguments for each comma‑separated element, so the command expands to file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly assigns the value 5 to a variable and then prints it?
questions.why: Variable assignment is done with NAME=value and the value is accessed with a preceding $. The first option follows this syntax.

questions.q: Which command correctly brings job number 3 to the foreground in a Bash shell?
questions.why: The fg builtin requires the job number preceded by a percent sign; fg %3 resumes job 3 in the foreground.

questions.q: If an interactive command is sent to the background and the shell cannot keep it there, what does the shell display?
questions.why: The shell stops the job and prints a message like "[1]+ Stopped command line here" indicating it is suspended.

questions.q: Within a screen session, which key sequence creates a new virtual window?
questions.why: Screen uses the control‑A prefix; pressing Ctrl‑C after it (Ctrl‑A Ctrl‑C) opens a new window.

questions.q: A script must create the full directory tree /var/www/site/data, creating any missing parent directories. Which command will accomplish this in one step?
questions.why: The -p option tells mkdir to create all missing parent directories along the specified path.

questions.q: You need to delete the empty directory hierarchy dir/a/b/c, removing each empty parent directory as well. Which command is appropriate?
questions.why: rmdir -p removes the specified directory and any empty parent directories automatically.

questions.q: To extract human‑readable text strings embedded in a compiled binary file named prog, which utility should you use?
questions.why: The strings command scans a binary file and prints sequences of printable characters.

questions.q: Which command should you use to start Vim with a graphical user interface on a Unix system?
questions.why: The 'gvim' command launches Vim in a new X window, providing a graphical interface.

questions.q: While editing in Vim, which key sequence returns you from insert mode to command mode?
questions.why: Pressing the Escape key exits insert mode and puts Vim back into command mode.

questions.q: What is the correct Vim command to write the current buffer to disk and then quit the editor?
questions.why: :wq writes the file and quits Vim; it combines saving and exiting in one command.

questions.q: A user runs `umask 0002` and then creates a regular file and a directory with the default creation modes. What permission bits will the new file and directory have?
options: rw-r--r-- for the file and rwxr-xr-x for the directory
rw-rw-r-- for the file and rwxrwxr-x for the directory
rw------- for the file and rwx------ for the directory
rwxrwxrwx for the file and rwxrwxrwx for the directory
questions.why: umask 0002 removes write permission for others only, so 666‑0002 = 664 (rw‑rw‑r--) and 777‑0002 = 775 (rwxrwxr-x).

questions.q: Which command will add both the compressed (c) and don’t‑dump (d) attributes to the file `data.txt`?
questions.why: The + operator adds attributes; `+cd` adds both compressed and don’t‑dump to the specified file.

questions.q: Setting the immutable (i) attribute on a file using `chattr` causes which of the following?
options: The file becomes hidden from directory listings
The file is automatically compressed on write
The file can be appended to but not overwritten
The file cannot be altered or removed, even by the root user
questions.why: The immutable attribute prevents any changes or deletion of the file, and this restriction applies to all users, including root.

questions.q: When creating a file name index with updatedb, which option tells the command to begin indexing from a specific directory and continue downward?
questions.why: The -U option specifies a directory from which updatedb should start indexing.

questions.q: Which locate command option makes the search ignore case differences in file names?
questions.why: The -i flag tells locate to perform a case‑insensitive search.

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between the 'type' and 'which' commands?
options: 'type' always lists every matching command in the PATH, while 'which' shows only the first.
'type' is a bash builtin and generally runs faster than the external 'which' program.
'type' is an external program located in /usr/bin, while 'which' is a shell builtin.
'which' can locate source code files, whereas 'type' can only find executables.
questions.why: 'type' is built into bash, making it faster than the external 'which' program.

questions.q:
A file contains the following lines:

2.5e2
300
1e3

Which sort command will correctly order these lines numerically, recognizing the scientific notation?
questions.why: The -g option performs a general numeric sort that understands scientific notation such as 2.5e2.

questions.q: You need to verify that a sorted file has no duplicate consecutive lines. Which command will cause an error if any duplicates are present?
questions.why: Combining -c (check order) with -u (unique) makes sort fail when duplicate consecutive lines exist.

questions.q: Given a CSV file "people" with lines like "Name,Street,City", which command will sort the entries alphabetically by the city field?
questions.why: The -t, option sets the comma as the field delimiter, and -k3 tells sort to use the third field (city) for ordering.

questions.q: Which diff option generates a context‑style diff that can be applied with the patch utility?
questions.why: The -c flag tells diff to produce a context diff, the format expected by patch.

questions.q: You need to compare two directory trees and see differences in all nested subdirectories. Which command will accomplish this?
questions.why: The -r option makes diff recurse into subdirectories, comparing the entire hierarchy.

questions.q: Which diff switch causes the comparison to ignore differences in letter case?
questions.why: The -i flag tells diff to ignore case when comparing text.

questions.q: You want to list all dictionary words that start with the letters "bi" using the look command. Which option correctly limits the prefix to characters up to "i"?
questions.why: The -t option tells look to stop matching at the termination character; using -t i with the prefix "bi" lists words beginning with "bi".

questions.q: Which aspell command will start an interactive spell‑checking session for the file report.txt?
questions.why: The -c option runs aspell in interactive mode, allowing the user to correct misspellings in the specified file.

questions.q: On a Linux system, the path /dev/sdb3 most likely refers to:
options: A regular text file containing disk usage statistics
A block device representing the third partition on the second SCSI/SATA drive
A network interface for the third Ethernet device
questions.why: /dev/sdb3 is a device file that represents the third partition of the second SCSI/SATA disk (sdb).

questions.q: Which option added to the ps command will cause the output to show a hierarchical view, indenting child processes beneath their parent processes?
questions.why: The -efH flags tell ps to list all processes in full format and display them in a tree (hierarchical) layout.

questions.q: Running the uptime command prints several pieces of information. Which of the following is NOT part of its normal output?
options: The number of users currently logged in
questions.why: Uptime shows time, uptime, user count, and load averages, but it does not report memory usage.

questions.q: In the output generated by the w command, what does the column labeled "JCPU" indicate?
options: The CPU time spent in kernel mode for that user
The total CPU time consumed by all of the user's processes
The CPU time used by processes attached to the user's terminal
The CPU time used by the most recent command the user ran
questions.why: JCPU reports the cumulative CPU time for all processes that are attached to the user's terminal (tty).

questions.q: When an at job is executed, which statement about its environment is correct?
options: The job starts with a completely empty environment.
The job always runs with the root user's environment variables.
The job inherits the current environment variables of the submitting user.
All user-defined aliases are available to the job.
questions.why: The at command preserves the current environment variables but does not include aliases.

questions.q: Which command installs an existing file named "mytasks" as your crontab schedule?
questions.why: Providing a filename without an option tells crontab to install that file as the user's crontab.

questions.q: Which of the following minute‑field specifications is invalid in a crontab entry?
questions.why: A step value of zero (*/0) is not allowed; the divisor must be a positive integer.

questions.q: You are creating a new account and need the user to be a member of the existing groups "audio" and "video" in addition to their primary group. Which useradd option should you use?
options: Use -G with a comma‑separated list of groups
Use -k to specify the group list
Use -g with a comma‑separated list of groups
Use -c to specify the group list
questions.why: The -G option adds the user to supplementary groups listed after it, separated by commas.

questions.q: When running "sudo userdel -r alice", what effect does the -r flag have?
options: It changes the user's default shell to /bin/false
It only deletes the user's mail spool file
It locks the account instead of deleting it
It removes the user's home directory and all its contents
questions.why: The -r option tells userdel to delete the user's home directory and its files along with the account.

questions.q: To rename the login name of an existing user from "bob" to "robert", which usermod option should be used, and what precaution is recommended?
options: Use -c to change the login name, and update the user's home directory afterwards
Use -l to change the login name, and verify that no scripts or services depend on the old name
Use -s to change the login name, and back up /etc/passwd first
Use -d to change the login name, and ensure the new name has a unique UID
questions.why: The -l option changes a user's login name; you should check for dependencies on the old name before renaming.

questions.q: Which command and option should you use to retrieve the MX (mail exchange) records for a domain?
questions.why: The host command with the -t MX option queries DNS for MX records, as shown in the example.

questions.q: When performing a whois lookup, how can you direct the query to a specific registrar's server?
questions.why: The -h option lets you specify the hostname of the whois server to query.

questions.q: Which ping option limits the number of echo request packets that are sent?
questions.why: The -c N option tells ping to send at most N packets before stopping.

questions.q: When using the Lynx text‑based web browser, which keystroke returns the cursor to the very beginning of the current document?
questions.why: ^A is defined in Lynx as the command to move to the top of the page.

questions.q: Which Lynx command‑line switch causes the program to print the formatted page to standard output and then quit?
questions.why: -dump tells Lynx to output the rendered page to stdout and exit.

questions.q: You started downloading a large file with wget but the connection dropped. Which option should you add to the same wget command to continue the download from where it stopped?
questions.why: -c enables wget’s continue mode, allowing a partially downloaded file to be resumed.

questions.q: Which printf format string will display a floating‑point number in a field eight characters wide, padded with leading zeros, and showing exactly two digits after the decimal point?
questions.why: The 0 flag adds leading zeros, 8 sets the minimum width, and .2 specifies two digits after the decimal point.

questions.q: You need to run a script called install.sh that asks for confirmation repeatedly. Which command will automatically supply a "yes" answer to every prompt?
questions.why: The yes command writes "y" repeatedly to its standard output, which can be piped into the script’s standard input.

questions.q: In the command wc -l notes.txt, what is -l?
options: An argument naming the file to read
An option that changes how the program behaves
questions.why: Options usually start with a dash and modify the program; here -l makes wc count lines. notes.txt is the argument and wc is the program.

questions.q: Which command is the same as wc -l -w file?
questions.why: Most programs accept single-letter options combined after one dash, so -lw equals -l -w. A few quirky programs don't support combining.

questions.q: What is the default shell for user accounts on most Linux distributions?
questions.why: bash, the Bourne-Again Shell, is the usual default. Other shells such as ksh and csh exist and share most basic features.

questions.q: Which file under /proc shows information about the system's processors?
questions.why: /proc/cpuinfo lists each CPU's model, speed and flags. /proc/version shows the kernel version and /proc/uptime the seconds since boot.

questions.q: What does /proc/self point to?
options: Information about the process reading it
questions.why: /proc/self is a symbolic link to /proc/<PID> of whichever process accesses it, so it changes every time a new command reads it.

questions.q: Which command prints the same kernel information as /proc/version?
questions.why: uname prints kernel name, release and version. uptime shows how long the system has run.

questions.q: Which operator sends a command's standard output to a file, replacing anything already in it?
questions.why: > creates or overwrites the file. >> appends, < reads standard input from a file and 2> redirects standard error.

questions.q: How do you append a command's output to the end of an existing file?
questions.why: >> adds to the end of the file instead of overwriting it, creating the file if it doesn't exist.

questions.q: How do you redirect only the error messages of a command to a file?
questions.why: File descriptor 2 is standard error. 2> sends it to the file while normal output still goes to the screen.

questions.q: Which redirects both standard output and standard error into a single file in bash?
questions.why: &> (or >& file, or > file 2>&1) sends both streams to the same file.

questions.q: What does the pipe in who | sort do?
options: Runs who and sort at random
Saves who's output to a file called sort
Sends who's output to sort as its input
Runs sort only if who fails
questions.why: The pipe connects one program's standard output to the next program's standard input, so sort receives the list of logged-in users.

questions.q: A long cat command is scrolling past. Which keystroke usually stops it?
questions.why: Ctrl+C sends an interrupt that ends the foreground program. Ctrl+Z suspends it and Ctrl+D sends end-of-file.

questions.q: How do you bring background job number 1 back to the foreground?
questions.why: fg resumes a job in the foreground. bg resumes a stopped job in the background and jobs lists them.

questions.q: After killing a program, your terminal no longer shows what you type. Which command usually restores it?
questions.why: reset reinitialises the terminal. Type it blind and press Ctrl+J (a newline) if Enter isn't working.

questions.q: Which cat option numbers every line of output?
questions.why: -n numbers all lines and -b numbers only non-blank ones. -s squeezes repeated blank lines and -E shows $ at line ends.

questions.q: Which command shows a text file one screen at a time and lets you scroll back?
questions.why: less is a pager that lets you scroll up and down and search with /. cat prints everything at once.

questions.q: In vim, which keys save the file and quit?
questions.why: :wq writes and quits. :q! quits without saving, and ZZ (not ZQ) also saves and quits.

questions.q: In vim, how do you leave insert mode?
questions.why: vim is modal: i enters insert mode for typing, and Esc returns to normal (command) mode.

questions.q: What does the sticky bit do when set on a directory such as /tmp?
options: Only a file's owner (or root) can delete or rename files in it
New files inherit the directory's group
Files in it run with the owner's privileges
questions.why: Normally write permission on a directory lets you delete any file in it. With the sticky bit, users can only remove their own files.

questions.q: With a umask of 0022, what permissions does a newly created regular file get?
questions.why: Files start from 0666 and the umask removes bits: 0666 minus 0022 leaves 0644. Directories start at 0777 and would get 0755.

questions.q: With a umask of 0002, what permission does a new directory get?
questions.why: Directories start from 0777; removing the 0002 bit (other-write) gives 0775, rwxrwxr-x.

questions.q: Why use find -print0 | xargs -0 instead of find -print | xargs?
options: It runs faster on large disks
It handles filenames that contain spaces correctly
questions.why: -print0 separates names with null characters and xargs -0 splits on them, so a file called my stuff isn't split into two arguments.

questions.q: Which xargs option runs the command once per input line?
questions.why: -n1 passes one argument to each run of the command. -0 changes the delimiter and -p asks before each run.

questions.q: Which command joins files side by side as columns?
questions.why: paste combines lines from several files into columns, separated by tabs by default. cut does the opposite and extracts columns.

questions.q: Which cut option sets the field delimiter?
questions.why: -d sets the delimiter character (tab by default) and -f picks the field numbers, as in cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd.

questions.q: Which command translates or deletes characters, for example converting lower case to upper case?
questions.why: tr maps one set of characters to another: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'. With -d it deletes characters.

questions.q: Which tar option creates a new archive?
questions.why: -c creates, -x extracts, -t lists the contents and -r appends files to an existing archive.

questions.q: What does tar -tzf backup.tar.gz do?
options: Tests the archive for errors and repairs it
Lists the contents of a gzip-compressed archive
questions.why: -t lists, -z handles gzip compression and -f names the archive file.

questions.q: Which tar option uses bzip2 compression?
questions.why: -j is bzip2, -z is gzip and -J is xz. -Z was old Unix compress.

questions.q: Which command creates a SHA-256 checksum of a file?
questions.why: SHA-256 is far more reliable than the old sum and cksum programs; md5sum works but MD5 is weak.

questions.q: How do you check files against a saved list of checksums?
questions.why: --check (-c) reads the saved sums, recomputes them and prints OK or FAILED for each file.

questions.q: When you run mount /usr with no device named, where does mount look up what to mount?
questions.why: mount reads /etc/fstab to find the device, filesystem type and options for that mount point.

questions.q: Which mount option mounts every filesystem listed in /etc/fstab?
questions.why: mount -a mounts all fstab entries except those marked noauto. It's also a good test that new fstab lines are valid.

questions.q: Why should you unmount a USB drive before removing it?
options: So cached writes are flushed and the filesystem is left consistent
questions.why: Linux caches writes. umount flushes them and marks the filesystem clean, so pulling the drive doesn't lose or corrupt data.

questions.q: Which command interactively shows the most active processes and refreshes every few seconds?
questions.why: top updates in place and lets you sort, renice and kill. ps shows a one-time snapshot.

questions.q: Which command schedules a one-time job, for example at 07:00 tomorrow?
questions.why: at runs a job once at the given time; atq lists queued jobs and atrm removes one. crontab is for recurring jobs.

questions.q: Which command edits your crontab?
questions.why: crontab -e opens your crontab in your editor and installs it on save. -l lists it and -r deletes it.

questions.q: How often does cron check for jobs that are due?
questions.why: The cron daemon wakes every minute, reads the crontabs and runs any job whose time matches.

questions.q: Which useradd option adds a user to extra groups?
questions.why: -G lists supplementary groups. -g sets the primary group, -m creates the home directory and -c sets the comment (full name).

questions.q: What does useradd -m do?
options: Creates the home directory and copies files from /etc/skel
questions.why: -m creates /home/<user> and copies the skeleton files such as .bashrc from /etc/skel.

questions.q: Which command deletes user smith and also removes the home directory?
questions.why: userdel alone leaves the home directory. -r removes it and the mail spool too.

questions.q: How do you lock a user account without deleting it?
questions.why: usermod -L puts a ! in front of the password hash so password logins fail, while files and the account remain.

questions.q: Which command shows the IP addresses on every interface?
questions.why: ip addr lists addresses per interface. ip route shows the routing table and ip link shows link-layer settings.

questions.q: Which command shows the routing table?
questions.why: ip route (ip r) lists destinations and gateways, including the default route.

questions.q: Which older command is the ancestor of ip and is now considered obsolete on many systems?
questions.why: ifconfig from net-tools still exists on many systems but ip from iproute2 replaces it and does much more.

questions.q: Which shell loop runs until its condition becomes true?
questions.why: until repeats while the test command returns non-zero (false) and stops when it succeeds. while is the opposite.

questions.q: What prints the numbers 1 to 5 in a bash for loop?
options: for i in $(seq 1 5); do echo $i; done
questions.why: seq generates the list and command substitution hands it to for. {1..5} brace expansion also works in bash.

questions.q: Which directory holds system-wide configuration files?
questions.why: /etc holds configuration as readable text, such as /etc/fstab and /etc/passwd. /var holds variable data like logs.

questions.q: What is in the /boot directory?
options: The kernel, initial RAM disk and boot loader files
questions.why: /boot contains vmlinuz (the kernel), the initramfs and GRUB's configuration.

questions.q: What does /dev contain?
options: Device nodes for the hardware the kernel knows about
questions.why: Following the everything-is-a-file idea, devices such as disks appear as files like /dev/sda.

questions.q: When you delete a symbolic link with rm, what is removed?
options: Only the link; the target stays
Both the link and the target
questions.why: Most operations follow a link to its target, but rm removes the link itself and leaves the file it points to.

questions.q: Which command removes a directory and everything inside it?
questions.why: rm -r recurses into subdirectories. rmdir only removes an empty directory.

questions.q: Which command removes duplicate adjacent lines, usually after sort?
questions.why: uniq drops repeated adjacent lines, so the input must be sorted first. uniq -d shows only the duplicates.

questions.q: What does wc print with no options?
questions.why: wc reports three counts: lines, words and bytes. -l, -w and -c select one.

questions.q: Where does bash keep your command history by default?
questions.why: bash writes the session's history to ~/.bash_history when you exit; history shows the list.

questions.q: Which command searches your history for previous commands that contained /usr/bin?
questions.why: Piping history into grep filters it; !88 would then re-run entry 88.

questions.q: Which command changes a file's owner to bob and its group to users?
questions.why: chown owner:group sets both. chown :group changes only the group, and chown bob: also sets bob's login group.

questions.q: Who can use chown to give a file to another user?
options: Any member of the file's group
questions.why: Giving away files is restricted to root so users can't dodge quotas or plant files as someone else.

questions.q: What does export do in bash?
options: Makes a variable available to programs started from the shell
questions.why: Exported variables become environment variables that child processes inherit; unexported ones stay in the shell.

questions.q: Which command prints the environment variables?
questions.why: printenv lists environment variables. set also shows shell variables and functions.

questions.q: In vi, which key opens a new line below the cursor and enters insert mode?
questions.why: o opens a line below and O opens one above; both switch to insert mode.

questions.q: In vi, what does dd do?
questions.why: d plus a movement deletes text; dd deletes the whole line and 5dd deletes five lines. x deletes one character.

questions.q: In vi, how do you undo the last change?
questions.why: u undoes the last change in normal mode. Ctrl+Z suspends the editor instead.

questions.q: Which file do you edit to make a custom PS1 prompt permanent for your user?
questions.why: ~/.bashrc runs for each interactive shell, so setting and exporting PS1 there keeps the prompt.

questions.q: What decides most of a distribution's quality according to experienced users, more than its desktop look?
questions.why: Software changes constantly, so how packages are managed and how active support is matters most day to day.

questions.q: Before running fdisk on a USB drive, what should you do?
questions.why: Partitioning a mounted device risks corruption, so umount /dev/sdb1 first, then run fdisk on the whole device, /dev/sdb.

questions.q: In fdisk, which command adds a new partition?
questions.why: n creates a partition, d deletes one, p prints the table and w writes changes and exits.

questions.q: What does fdisk's q command do?
questions.why: Nothing is written until w. q leaves without changing the disk.

questions.q: What does ssh warn you about when a server's host key has changed?
options: The remote host's identity may have changed, possibly an attack
questions.why: ssh stores host keys in known_hosts. A changed key could mean a reinstall, or someone intercepting the connection.

questions.q: How do you log in to a remote system as a different user, bob?
questions.why: user@host tells ssh which account to use; ssh -l bob remote-sys works too.

questions.q: Which command shows all of a file's timestamps, inode and permissions?
questions.why: stat shows access, modify and change times, inode number, links and permissions in detail.

questions.q: What does touch do to an existing file?
questions.why: touch sets the access and modification times to the current time; on a missing file it creates an empty one.

questions.q: What does rsync --delete do?
options: Deletes files older than a week
Removes files at the destination that no longer exist at the source
questions.why: --delete makes the destination an exact mirror of the source, which is useful for backups but dangerous if paths are wrong.

questions.q: What does the r in rsync stand for?
questions.why: rsync can copy over a network via ssh, transferring only the differences between files.

questions.q: Which locate option enables extended regular expressions?
questions.why: --regex uses extended regular expressions and --regexp uses basic ones.

questions.q: In less, how do you search forward for a pattern?
questions.why: /pattern searches forward and n jumps to the next match. ? searches backward.

questions.q: Which diff option produces the unified format used by patches?
questions.why: -u gives unified output with + and - lines. -c is the context format and -q only says whether files differ.

questions.q: In default diff output, what does 1d0 mean?
options: Line 1 of the first file must be deleted
questions.why: Default diff uses commands such as a (append), c (change) and d (delete) to turn the first file into the second.

questions.q: What does the nl command do?
questions.why: nl numbers lines, by default only non-blank ones (-b t). -b a numbers all lines.

questions.q: Why are terminals traditionally 80 characters wide?
options: Printers printed about 80 characters across a page
questions.why: At 10 characters per inch on letter paper, with margins, 80 characters was the widest print line.

questions.q: In a makefile, what does CC= gcc set?
questions.why: Variables like CC are substituted later, so $(CC) becomes gcc when make runs.

questions.q: What is top-down design?
options: Breaking a large task into steps, then each step into smaller ones
Writing code from the last line up
Testing a program before writing it
questions.why: Top-down design keeps refining high-level steps into small tasks, which suits shell scripts built from functions.

questions.q: What does [ -d temp ] || exit 1 do in a script?
options: Exits with status 1 if the directory temp doesn't exist
questions.why: || runs the second command only if the first fails, so a missing temp directory ends the script.

questions.q: What does id -u print?
options: The numeric user ID of the effective user
questions.why: id -u prints the UID; root is always 0, so scripts compare it with 0 to check for superuser rights.

questions.q: Why can [ $number = 1 ] fail with 'unary operator expected'?
options: If number is empty, the test becomes [ = 1 ]
questions.why: An empty variable vanishes on expansion. Quoting it, [ "$number" = 1 ], keeps an empty string in place.

questions.q: What is the general rule for quoting variables in shell scripts?
options: Double-quote variables and command substitutions unless you want word splitting
questions.why: Double quotes stop empty values from vanishing and names with spaces from splitting into several words.

questions.q: In a script's option loop, what does shift do?
options: Moves the positional parameters left so $2 becomes $1
Runs the next command in the background
questions.why: shift drops $1 and moves the rest down, so a while loop can process arguments one at a time until none remain.

questions.q: What does read -p "Name: " name do?
options: Shows a prompt and stores the user's input in name
questions.why: read takes a line from standard input; -p prints a prompt first.

questions.q: In bash arithmetic, what does (( 0 )) return as an exit status?
questions.why: (( )) maps arithmetic results to exit codes: a non-zero result is success (0) and zero is failure (1).

questions.q: Why give temporary files unpredictable names?
options: To prevent temp race attacks in shared /tmp
questions.why: If an attacker can guess the name, they can create it first as a link to something sensitive. mktemp makes safe names.

questions.q: Which command creates a temporary file with a random, safe name?
questions.why: mktemp replaces the X characters in its template with random letters and creates the file securely.

questions.q: Which command lists block devices such as disks and partitions in a tree?
questions.why: lsblk shows disks, partitions and their mount points. lsmod lists kernel modules and lsof open files.

questions.q: Which command shows how much space is free on each mounted filesystem?
questions.why: df reports filesystem usage; -h prints sizes in human-readable units. du measures directory sizes instead.

questions.q: Which command shows the total size of a directory?
questions.why: du -s summarises the total and -h makes it readable, such as 1.2G.

questions.q: Which command shows memory and swap usage?
questions.why: free shows total, used and available RAM and swap; -h uses human-readable units.

questions.q: Which ps command lists every process on the system with full details?
questions.why: ps aux shows all users' processes with CPU, memory and command line. Plain ps shows only your terminal's processes.

questions.q: Which signal does kill send by default?
questions.why: SIGTERM asks the process to exit cleanly. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which can't be caught, so use it only as a last resort.

questions.q: Which command runs a program with a lower scheduling priority?
questions.why: nice starts a command with an adjusted niceness; higher values mean lower priority. renice changes a running process.

questions.q: Which command keeps a program running after you log out?
questions.why: nohup ignores the hangup signal sent at logout, and & puts the job in the background.

questions.q: Which grep option searches recursively through directories?
questions.why: -r recurses. -i ignores case, -v inverts the match and -c counts matching lines.

questions.q: Which grep option shows lines that do not match the pattern?
questions.why: -v inverts the match. -l lists only file names and -n adds line numbers.

questions.q: Which command finds files under /home larger than 100 MB?
questions.why: find tests attributes; -size +100M means more than 100 megabytes.

questions.q: Which find test finds files modified within the last day?
questions.why: -mtime -1 means modified less than one day ago; +1 means more than one day ago.

questions.q: Which command changes a file so its owner can read, write and execute and no one else has any access?
questions.why: 7 is rwx for the owner and 0 removes everything for group and others. 600 would give rw without execute.

questions.q: What does chmod u+x script.sh do?
options: Adds execute permission for the file's owner
Makes the script run as root
questions.why: Symbolic mode: u is the user who owns the file, + adds and x is execute.

questions.q: Which line at the top of a script tells the system to run it with bash?
questions.why: The shebang (#!) names the interpreter the kernel should use when the file is run directly.

questions.q: Which variable holds the exit status of the last command?
questions.why: $? is 0 for success and non-zero for failure. $$ is the shell's PID, $! the last background PID and $# the argument count.

questions.q: Which variable holds the number of arguments passed to a script?
questions.why: $# counts the positional parameters. $@ and $* expand to the arguments themselves and $0 is the script name.

questions.q: Which command makes ls -la available as ll for the current session?
questions.why: alias defines a shortcut; put it in ~/.bashrc to keep it across sessions.

questions.q: Which command shows where a command's executable is in your PATH?
questions.why: which searches PATH and prints the first matching executable. type also tells you if it's an alias or builtin.

questions.q: Which command displays the manual page for a command?
questions.why: man shows the manual. For bash builtins, help gives built-in documentation.

questions.q: Which archive command compresses a file, replacing it with file.gz?
questions.why: gzip compresses in place and removes the original; gunzip reverses it and zcat prints the content without decompressing to disk.

questions.q: Which command copies a directory and its contents?
questions.why: cp needs -r (or -a to preserve attributes) to copy directories recursively.

questions.q: What does ln -s target linkname create?
questions.why: -s makes a symbolic (soft) link, a pointer to a path. Without -s, ln creates a hard link to the same inode.

questions.q: What is a difference between hard links and symbolic links?
options: A symlink keeps the data if the target is deleted
Hard links can point to directories freely
A hard link can't span filesystems; a symlink can
questions.why: Hard links are extra names for the same inode on one filesystem. Symlinks store a path, which can be anywhere but breaks if the target goes.

questions.q: Which command shows the last 20 lines of a log and keeps printing new lines as they arrive?
questions.why: tail -f follows the file as it grows, which is how admins watch logs live.

questions.q: Which sort option sorts numerically rather than alphabetically?
questions.why: -n compares numbers, so 10 comes after 9. -r reverses, -u removes duplicates and -k picks a field.
